title: Primality testing: trial division vs AKS
problem_statement: Given an integer N >= 0, decide whether N is prime.

input.size_measure: n bits (the standard binary encoding of N).

algorithms.name: trial division
algorithms.idea: Try every odd divisor d with d^2 <= N.
algorithms.pseudocode: if N < 2: no; if N even: N == 2; for d = 3, 5, 7, ... while d*d <= N: if d | N: no; yes
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(sqrt(N)) = Theta(2^(n/2)) divisions in the worst case (N prime): exactly 1 + floor((floor(sqrt N) - 1)/2) divisions on an odd prime N and at most that many on any N >= 2; n-bit primes exist for every n >= 2 (Bertrand's postulate, proved in PROOFS.md)
algorithms.correctness: A composite N has a divisor d with 1 < d <= sqrt(N).

algorithms.name: AKS
algorithms.idea: N is prime iff (X + a)^N = X^N + a mod (X^r - 1, N) for a small r and few a, after ruling out perfect powers and small factors. Working modulo X^r - 1 keeps polynomials of degree < r <= max(16, n (n^2 + 1)^2) = O(n^5).
algorithms.pseudocode: see implementation (the six steps of AKS 2004, with log2 N replaced in steps 2 and 5 by an exact rational upper bound lam, log2 N <= lam <= n)
algorithms.time_complexity: Õ(n^(21/2)) bit operations when multiplication and division of m-bit integers cost Õ(m), and O(n^(33/2)) with schoolbook integer arithmetic: polynomial, for this implementation. On every n-bit prime with n >= 24 it performs at least (n - 1)^4 n coefficient operations (Omega(n^5)). Faster analyses and the Lenstra-Pomerance variant: see background.
algorithms.space_complexity: O(n^6) bits (polynomials with r coefficients of O(n) bits, r = O(n^5))
algorithms.correctness: Returns True iff N is prime, for every N >= 0 (proved in PROOFS.md, Part A, following Agrawal, Kayal, Saxena 2004).

relationship: Trial division is exponential in the input size n (Theta(2^(n/2)) divisions in the worst case); AKS is polynomial in n. Same problem, same deterministic model.

sources.authors: Agrawal, M.; Kayal, N.; Saxena, N.
sources.title: PRIMES is in P

sources.authors: Lenstra, H. W., Jr.; Pomerance, C.
sources.title: Primality testing with Gaussian periods
sources.venue: Journal of the European Mathematical Society 21(4), 1229-1269

sources.title: Strong pseudoprimes to twelve prime bases
sources.note: Background only: Theorem 1.1 gives psi_12 = 318665857834031151167461, the smallest strong pseudoprime to the first twelve prime bases (and psi_13); the bound used by the V2 generator's deterministic Miller-Rabin test.

sources.title: On Chebyshev-type inequalities for primes
sources.note: Credit for the lower bound lcm(1, ..., m) >= 2^m used in PROOFS.md, Lemma A2 (proved there).

verification.method: Both implementations agree with each other and with a sieve-of-Eratosthenes oracle on random n-bit integers (each one a uniformly chosen n-bit prime with probability 1/2, otherwise a uniform n-bit integer), n = 0..20 (AKS up to 16 bits, where step 5 is genuinely exercised: N > r). Trial division's 2^(n/2) scaling is measured; AKS scaling is not (its polynomial only dominates far beyond what pure Python can time), so the pair stays at V1. Proofs: PROOFS.md proves every claim of this entry (trial division's correctness, exact division counts and worst case; the correctness of the AKS implementation for every N, the bound on r, its polynomial time and space bounds and a lower bound on primes; the harness facts) and names the deterministic tests that check each one.

caveats: AKS matters for theory: its proved running time is a polynomial of high degree, and on every n-bit prime with n >= 24 it performs Omega(n^5) operations, against O(n^3) bit operations per round for the randomized Miller-Rabin test (primality-miller-rabin-vs-aks). 'Exponential' for trial division refers to the bit length n. Trial division is polynomial in the value N (O(sqrt N) divisions), which is exponentially larger than the input.
notes: See primality-miller-rabin-vs-aks for the randomized-vs-deterministic (T4) view of the same problem.

background.statement: Agrawal, Kayal and Saxena give an unconditional deterministic polynomial-time primality test.

Lenstra and Pomerance give a deterministic primality test that runs in time (log N)^6 (2 + log log N)^c for an effectively computable constant c; according to their abstract, the same result with 21/2 in place of 6 was proved by Agrawal, Kayal and Saxena.

The V2 generator's Miller-Rabin test with the twelve prime bases 2, ..., 37 is used only below 318665857834031151167461 = 399165290221 * 798330580441, which Sorenson and Webster prove to be psi_12, the smallest strong pseudoprime to the first twelve prime bases, so the test is exact below it (cited, not proved here; that this number is composite and passes all twelve bases is checked in tests/test_proofs_primality.py). The V2 instances (n <= 40 bits) are checked prime by trial division in tests/test_proofs_primality.py.
